questions.q:
A trainee volunteer at a health camp in a Nashik village filled in this record.
Patient | Problem | Volunteer's entry
K | Goitre; swelling noticed 2 weeks ago | Communicable; isolate the patient from family
L | Asthma for 4 years | Non-communicable; chronic
M | Cough and fever for 3 weeks | Non-communicable; chronic
The volunteer now wants to give all three patients the same advice: 'Eat a balanced diet with plenty of fruits, vegetables and whole grains.'
(a) What is wrong with the entry for patient K?
(b) M's cough and fever could be a communicable disease from the chapter's table. Name one such disease and say why both words in M's entry are not supported.
(c) Is L's entry correct? Give the reason.
(d) For which patient does the volunteer's diet advice supply exactly what the body is lacking, and so remove the cause of the disease? Why does it not meet M's need?
questions.a: (a) Goitre is a deficiency disease, caused by a lack of specific nutrients in the diet. It is non-communicable, so isolation is not needed. (b) Tuberculosis (cough, fever, caused by bacteria, communicable); influenza, also with cough and fever and caused by a virus, is accepted. So 'non-communicable' may be wrong, and 'chronic' is not supported because chronic diseases persist for more than 3 months and M has been ill for 3 weeks. (c) Yes. Asthma is a non-communicable disease, and lasting 4 years (more than 3 months) makes it chronic. (d) K, because goitre is caused by a lack of specific nutrients (asthma is linked to lifestyle, diet or environment but is not caused by a missing nutrient), so a diet that supplies them removes the cause. M may have a disease caused by a pathogen such as TB bacteria, which a diet does not remove; M needs to see a doctor, and others should avoid close contact and cover the mouth and nose.
s: Part (a): goitre is a non-communicable deficiency disease, so isolation is wrong
Part (b): any communicable disease from Table 3.1 with cough and fever (TB or influenza); 3 weeks is not more than 3 months
Part (c): correct; NCD lasting 4 years
Part (d): K, as diet supplies the missing nutrient; M may have a pathogen that diet does not remove

questions.q: A news clipping says 11.4% of India's population is diabetic. If a housing society of 2,500 residents had exactly the same share, ___ residents would be diabetic. (Write the number in digits.)

Mr Bhatt, 48, drives everywhere, eats sweets and fried snacks every day and is overweight. His doctor also finds that some of his hormones are out of balance. A lab test finds no pathogen. Which disease does the chapter say often develops from exactly this combination of causes?
questions.a: Diabetes
o: Diabetes
Anaemia
Tuberculosis
Asthma

questions.q: Differentiate between a deficiency disease and a chronic disease such as diabetes, giving one example of each. Then state what the two have in common.
questions.a: A deficiency disease is caused by a lack of specific nutrients in the diet, e.g. scurvy, anaemia or goitre. A chronic disease is one that often persists for a long time (more than 3 months), e.g. diabetes, cancer or asthma, and diabetes is linked to hormones, eating habits, physical activity and weight. Common: both are non-communicable; they are not caused by pathogens and do not spread from person to person.
s: The difference, with one example of each
Both are non-communicable (no pathogen, do not spread)

questions.q: Ramesh and his father live in the same house. Both have had diabetes for years. A neighbour says: 'One of them must have given it to the other.' A Class 8 student replies: 'Two people in the same house can have the same disease for years without either having given it to the other.' Is the student's statement True or False? Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Diabetes is a non-communicable disease: it is not caused by a pathogen and does not spread from one person to another. Both can have it because of causes such as hormonal imbalance, unhealthy eating habits, lack of physical activity or being overweight, which a family living together may share, and it lasts a long time (a chronic disease).
s: Verdict: True
Reason: diabetes is non-communicable (no pathogen, does not spread); shared causes such as eating habits or inactivity explain both cases

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Scurvy is a communicable disease, because many people in the same village can have it at the same time.
Reason (R): Deficiency diseases are caused by a lack of specific nutrients in the diet.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q: A parent at a school meeting claims: 'Diabetes is a disease of old people, so children do not need to worry about what they eat or how active they are.' Check the claim against the chapter.
questions.a: Wrong. The chapter says diabetes is becoming more prevalent in adults as well as children. It often develops from unhealthy eating habits, lack of physical activity and being overweight or obese (along with hormonal imbalances), so children's diet and activity do matter.
s: Verdict: wrong
Diabetes is rising in children as well as adults
Its causes include eating habits, inactivity and obesity, which apply to children

questions.q: A Class 8 group is listing reasons why non-communicable diseases like diabetes and heart disease have become more common in India. Which reason should they NOT include?
questions.a: More pathogens now spread through crowded cities
o: More pathogens now spread through crowded cities
People are eating more processed food than before
People are getting less exercise in daily life
People are living longer lives than they used to

questions.q: 'Most non-communicable diseases in India grow out of the way we live, so the way we live can also hold them back.' Justify this statement in four points using the chapter, and then give one limit to it.
questions.a: (1) NCDs such as diabetes, heart disease and cancer are linked to lifestyle, diet and environment, not to pathogens. (2) They have become more common in India because people eat more processed food and get less exercise. (3) Diabetes often develops from unhealthy eating habits, lack of physical activity and being overweight or obese, all of which come from the way we live. (4) The chapter says NCDs can often be prevented with healthy habits, lifestyle changes and regular exercise, and lifestyle change is also part of their treatment. Limit (any one from the chapter): hormonal imbalances also cause diabetes; people living longer lives is one reason NCDs have become more common, and that is not a habit to give up.
s: NCDs are linked to lifestyle, diet and environment, not pathogens
They are rising with processed food and less exercise
Diabetes links to eating habits, inactivity and being overweight
Healthy habits can prevent and help treat NCDs
One limit the chapter gives: hormonal imbalance or living longer

questions.q:
Ravi, 14, is overweight. He drinks two bottles of sweet cola a day, eats chips every evening and spends his free time on video games.
(a) Name two causes of diabetes from the chapter that his routine shows.
(b) Explain why each cause in (a) is a lifestyle factor rather than an infection, and so what kind of change could lower his risk.
questions.a: (a) Any two: unhealthy eating habits (cola, chips), lack of physical activity (games instead of play), being overweight or obese. (b) Each comes from how he lives (what he eats and how active he is), not from a pathogen, so no medicine against germs or vaccine can remove it. Changing his own habits can: avoiding sugary and processed food and drinks in favour of a balanced diet, and staying physically active by playing outdoors, walking or cycling instead of sitting at games.
s: Part (a): two causes from his routine
Part (b): they come from how he lives, not pathogens, so changing diet and activity lowers his risk

questions.q:
A Class 8 in a Bhopal school surveyed all 40 students. 12 students were overweight; 10 of these 12 ate packaged chips, fried snacks or sugary drinks on at least four days a week. Of the other 28 students, 6 ate such food that often. The survey also found that 75% of the overweight students, and 25% of the others, exercised less than one hour a week.
(a) What percentage of the overweight students, and of the other students, ate such food often? Round each to the nearest whole number.
(b) Name the non-communicable disease for which the chapter gives being overweight as a cause, and say which other causes of it the overweight students in this survey show.
(c) The school can afford only one change this year: replace the canteen's chips and sugary drinks with fruit and whole-grain snacks, or add a daily 30-minute outdoor games period. Weigh the two using the survey figures and decide; either choice can earn full marks if it is argued from the data.
questions.a: (a) Overweight: 10 / 12 x 100 = 83%. Others: 6 / 28 x 100 = 21%. (b) Diabetes. The overweight students also show unhealthy eating habits and lack of physical activity, the other two lifestyle causes the chapter names. (c) Either choice is accepted when it uses the figures and recognises the other option's case. For the canteen: the eating gap is larger (83% against 21%, 62 points), and the change alters what students actually eat at school every day. For the games period: 75% of the overweight students hardly exercise against 25% of the others (a 50-point gap), the chapter asks us to stay physically active, and a canteen change does not stop students buying the same snacks outside school. Both target a cause of diabetes, so the option not chosen should follow next year.
s: Part (a): 83% and 21%
Part (b): diabetes; the survey also shows unhealthy eating and inactivity
Part (c): either choice, argued from the survey figures (62-point eating gap, 50-point exercise gap), with the other option's case acknowledged

questions.q: Mr Pillai has had asthma for six years. He says, 'I must have caught it from my neighbour, who also has asthma.' Which statement correctly answers him?
questions.a: Asthma is not caused by a pathogen, so it does not pass between people
o: Asthma is not caused by a pathogen, so it does not pass between people
He is right, because asthma spreads through the air like influenza does
He is right, but only if the two of them shared towels and handkerchiefs
Asthma is caused by worms, so he caught it from soil and not his neighbour

questions.q: Asha's grandmother has just been told she has diabetes. Her uncle says: 'No single course of medicine will cure it, so the monthly visits to the doctor are a waste. We should take her only when she becomes very ill.' Evaluate the uncle's plan in three steps, using what the chapter says about treating non-communicable diseases.
questions.a: (1) His premise is right but his conclusion is wrong: therapy for non-communicable diseases is not a quick cure; it aims at managing symptoms and improving quality of life. (2) That management needs medication along with lifestyle changes and rehabilitation, which have to be kept up and adjusted over time, so regular visits are part of the treatment. (3) The chapter says early diagnosis and continuous care are key to controlling the progress of the disease and preventing complications; waiting until she is very ill gives up exactly that, so the plan risks complications.
s: No quick cure, but treatment manages symptoms and improves quality of life
Medication, lifestyle change and rehabilitation need ongoing care
Continuous care controls progress and prevents complications, which waiting would lose

questions.q:
Twenty-five years ago most deaths in Mr Rao's district were from cholera and typhoid. Today most deaths there are from heart disease and diabetes.
(a) Classify the two groups of diseases, and give one change in the way people live that the chapter blames for the rise of the second group.
(b) Mr Rao says: 'The district should keep spending its whole health budget on clean drinking water, since that is what saved lives before.' Judge his plan.
questions.a: (a) Cholera and typhoid are communicable (caused by bacteria and spread through contaminated water and food); heart disease and diabetes are non-communicable. Any one cause: eating more processed food, getting less exercise, living longer lives. (b) Not a good plan on its own. Clean, boiled drinking water prevents water-borne communicable diseases like cholera and typhoid, but heart disease and diabetes are not caused by pathogens and are linked to lifestyle and diet, so clean water cannot hold them back; money is also needed for healthy habits such as a balanced diet and physical activity, and for early diagnosis.
s: Part (a): first group communicable, second non-communicable, with one lifestyle cause
Part (b): clean water stops water-borne diseases but not NCDs, which need lifestyle measures

questions.q: A village leader proposes a vaccination camp to get rid of goitre and scurvy in the village. Show why a vaccine cannot prevent these diseases, and say what kind of step would.
questions.a: A vaccine trains the immune system to recognise and attack harmful germs (pathogens). Goitre and scurvy are deficiency diseases: they are caused by a lack of specific nutrients in the diet, not by any pathogen, so there is nothing for the immune system to fight. They are prevented by a diet that supplies the missing nutrients.
s: Vaccines train the immune system against pathogens
Goitre and scurvy are caused by a lack of nutrients, not pathogens
The fix is a diet that provides the missing nutrients

questions.q:
A diabetes screening camp in Surat records three adults who feel healthy.
Person | Weight | Exercise | Food habits
Mr Shah | Normal | None; drives everywhere | Sweets and fried snacks daily
Ms Desai | Normal | Walks 40 minutes daily | Home-cooked meals with vegetables
Mr Patel | Overweight | Walks 30 minutes daily | Sweets and fried snacks daily
The camp's rule is: 'Send only overweight people for a blood-sugar test.'
(a) The chapter names three lifestyle causes of diabetes: unhealthy eating habits, lack of physical activity and being overweight or obese. How many of the three does each person's row show?
(b) Ms Desai says: 'My row shows none of the causes, so I can never get diabetes.' Judge her claim using the chapter.
(c) Why does the camp not need to keep these three people apart from each other?
(d) Use the table to find the flaw in the camp's rule, and suggest a fairer rule.
questions.a: (a) Mr Shah 2 (no physical activity, unhealthy eating); Ms Desai 0; Mr Patel 2 (overweight, unhealthy eating). (b) Not right. Diabetes often develops from a combination of hormonal imbalances, unhealthy eating, inactivity, being overweight and other reasons; hormonal imbalance cannot be seen in this table, so her row lowers her risk but cannot rule diabetes out. (c) Diabetes is a non-communicable disease: it is not caused by a pathogen and does not spread from one person to another. (d) The rule would test Mr Patel but miss Mr Shah, whose row shows just as many causes (2 of 3) though his weight is normal. Diabetes comes from a combination of causes, so weight alone is a poor filter. A fairer rule: test anyone whose row shows two or more of the lifestyle causes (here Shah and Patel).
s: Part (a): Shah 2, Desai 0, Patel 2
Part (b): not right; hormonal imbalance and other reasons cannot be seen in the table
Part (c): diabetes is non-communicable, not caused by a pathogen
Part (d): the rule misses Shah, who has as many causes as Patel; test by number of causes, not weight alone

questions.q:
The Iyer family's health card lists:
Dadaji: diabetes for 8 years
Amma: anaemia found in a blood test; her meals have very little variety
Varun: typhoid last month, now cured
Aunt Lalitha: asthma for 3 years; she lives beside a cement factory
(a) Group each member's disease as communicable or non-communicable. (2)
(b) Which of the non-communicable diseases are chronic, and which one is a deficiency disease? (2)
(c) For Aunt Lalitha, which factor named in the chapter is likely making her condition worse? (1)
questions.a: (a) Communicable: Varun's typhoid (caused by bacteria). Non-communicable: Dadaji's diabetes, Amma's anaemia and Aunt Lalitha's asthma. (b) Chronic: diabetes (8 years) and asthma (3 years), both lasting more than 3 months. Deficiency disease: Amma's anaemia, caused by a lack of specific nutrients in her diet. (c) Her environment: air pollution from the factory, which can cause coughing or asthma.
s: Typhoid is communicable
Diabetes, anaemia and asthma are non-communicable
Diabetes and asthma are chronic (over 3 months)
Anaemia is the deficiency disease
Polluted air from the factory (environment)

questions.q:
Before a trip, a school nurse in Shimla checks five students' records. A measles case has just been reported in the town.
Student | Measles vaccine taken? | Measles history
A | Yes | Never had measles
B | No | Never had measles
C | No | Sick with measles right now
D | No | Had measles at age 5, recovered
E | No | Never had measles
The nurse has two doses of measles vaccine. Her assistant proposes: 'Give one dose to C, so C recovers before the trip, and one to D, because protection that came from an illness is weaker than protection from a vaccine.'
(a) Which two students already have acquired immunity to measles, and how did each get it?
(b) Why would giving C a dose today not help C get well?
(c) Which students are neither protected against measles nor already ill with it?
(d) Evaluate both reasons in the assistant's proposal and say who should get the two doses.
questions.a: (a) A, from the vaccine, and D, from exposure to the measles pathogen when D had the disease; acquired immunity is protection developed after exposure to a pathogen or a vaccine. (b) Vaccines are preventive, not curative: they help prevent a disease before it happens but do not treat someone who is already sick. C needs care and isolation instead. (c) B and E (A and D are protected; C is already ill). (d) Both reasons are wrong. The dose cannot make C recover, because a vaccine does not treat a disease already present. The chapter counts protection after exposure to a pathogen as acquired immunity, just like protection from a vaccine, so D is already protected and gains nothing. The two doses should go to B and E, who are unprotected and still well, so a vaccine can train their immune systems before they meet the virus.
s: Part (a): A from the vaccine, D from having had measles
Part (b): vaccines are preventive, not curative
Part (c): B and E
Part (d): both reasons fail (no cure for C; D already has acquired immunity), so B and E get the doses

questions.q: Two sisters live in the same house, eat the same food and go to the same school. Meenu catches colds several times every winter; Neha rarely falls ill. According to the chapter, what best explains the difference?
questions.a: Their bodies differ in natural ability to fight disease
o: Their bodies differ in natural ability to fight disease
Neha once took antibiotics, which now block every cold for her
Meenu's colds are a deficiency disease caused by her diet
Neha's measles vaccine also protects her from colds

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A child vaccinated against measles is protected from it even though she has never had measles.
Reason (R): A vaccine trains the immune system to recognise and attack the germ, giving acquired immunity.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: A new vaccine contains no germs at all, alive or dead. A parent at a Nashik clinic asks how it can still protect her child. Which explanation fits the chapter?
questions.a: Body cells make a harmless germ part that the immune system learns
o: Body cells make a harmless germ part that the immune system learns
It kills germs directly in the blood, in the way an antibiotic does
It makes the body's cells resistant, as bacteria become resistant
It works only once the child has caught the disease and is sick

questions.q:
Riya caught measles when she was four and recovered. Her cousin Sunil never had measles but was given the measles vaccine.
(a) Do both of them have acquired immunity to measles?
(b) Using the chapter's meaning of acquired immunity, explain how each of them got it.
questions.a: (a) Yes, both. (b) Acquired immunity is protection developed after exposure to a pathogen or a vaccine. Riya got it from exposure to the measles pathogen itself (by having the disease); Sunil got it from the vaccine, which trained his immune system without his having the disease.
s: Part (a): yes, both
Part (b): Riya from the pathogen, Sunil from the vaccine

questions.q: In Class 6B, 38 of the 40 children have had the measles vaccine; Aarav and Bina have not. Bina says: 'The vaccine only protects the children who took it, so the other 38 being vaccinated does nothing for Aarav and me.' A classmate replies: 'Aarav and Bina are safer in this class than they would be in a class where few children are vaccinated.' Is the classmate's statement True or False? Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Getting vaccinated protects not only the vaccinated person but also the people around them. Measles spreads from person to person, and vaccinated children are protected, so they are unlikely to catch it and pass it on. With 38 of 40 vaccinated, there are few people through whom measles could reach Aarav and Bina; vaccines reduce the spread of infections. (They are still not as safe as if they took the vaccine themselves.)
s: Verdict: True
Reason: vaccinated classmates rarely catch and pass on measles, so vaccination protects the people around them too

questions.q: A doctor notes that when Arif's body met a particular pathogen for the second time, its immune response was far stronger than the first time. What is the best name for the protection built up in this way?
questions.a: Acquired immunity
o: Acquired immunity
Antibiotic resistance
Curative treatment
A deficiency disease

questions.q: Riya's vaccination card lists vaccines against measles, typhoid, tetanus, hepatitis A and tuberculosis. Of these five, the number that protect her against a disease caused by bacteria is ___. (Write the number in digits.)
After a tetanus shot for a cut, Vivek claims: 'Now my immune system is trained, so I am protected against every disease, including flu and typhoid.' Check his claim.
questions.a: Wrong. A vaccine helps the body fight certain diseases by training the immune system to recognise and attack particular harmful germs. The tetanus shot protects against the tetanus-causing bacteria only. Flu and typhoid are caused by different pathogens, so he is not protected against them by this shot.
s: Verdict: wrong
A vaccine trains the immune system against particular germs only
The tetanus shot protects against tetanus, not flu or typhoid

questions.q:
Read three statements about vaccines and immunity.
Statement 1: A vaccine can be made from inactive or harmless parts of a pathogen.
Statement 2: When the body meets the same pathogen a second time, its immune response is usually weaker than the first time.
Statement 3: Vaccines are meant for infants only; adults gain nothing from them.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
All three statements

questions.q: Seven-year-old Kiran already has fever and red rashes from measles. Her uncle suggests taking her for the measles vaccine at once so that she recovers faster. Which reply is correct?
questions.a: A vaccine prevents illness; it will not treat what she has
o: A vaccine prevents illness; it will not treat what she has
Yes, a vaccine works fastest once the rashes have appeared
Yes, but only a vaccine made from dead measles viruses
No, because vaccines work only against bacterial infections

questions.q:
A doctor's notes on Arif: at age 4 he caught chickenpox for the first time; his immune response was low and he was ill for over a week. At age 9 his sister had chickenpox in the same room, and the doctor found Arif's immune response to the same virus much stronger; he did not fall ill.
(i) Explain why his body responded so much more strongly the second time.
(ii) Name the kind of immunity he showed at age 9.
(iii) Use this to explain how a vaccine can protect a child who has never had chickenpox.
questions.a: (i) The first exposure trained his immune system to recognise and attack the chickenpox virus, so on meeting the same pathogen again it responded quickly and strongly before the virus could make him ill. (ii) Acquired immunity: protection developed after exposure to a pathogen. (iii) A vaccine gives the immune system its 'first exposure' safely, using weakened or dead pathogens or harmless parts of them. The child's immune system learns to recognise the germ, so when the real virus comes it responds as strongly as Arif's did the second time, without the child first having the disease.
s: The first exposure trained the immune system to recognise the virus
Acquired immunity, developed after exposure to a pathogen
A vaccine provides a safe first exposure, so the response to the real virus is strong

questions.q:
A tetanus shot is often given to someone right after an injury.
(a) The chapter calls vaccines preventive. Explain why giving the shot after the injury is still prevention and not a cure.
(b) The shot contains a bacterial toxin. Explain why the toxin must be inactivated rather than active.
questions.a: (a) The injury is not the disease. The shot is given before the tetanus-causing bacteria can produce an infection, and it protects against that infection; it does not treat a tetanus disease that has already developed. (b) An active toxin would harm the body and cause the disease. An inactivated toxin can still train the immune system to develop protection, but without causing the disease.
s: Part (a): the shot protects before the infection develops, so it prevents rather than cures
Part (b): an active toxin would cause disease; inactivated, it builds protection without it

questions.q:
Match each vaccine description in Column I with the way it is made in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. The tetanus shot given after an injury | a. Made from pathogens that have been killed
2. A vaccine containing germs that are no longer alive | b. Makes the body's own cells produce a harmless part of the germ
3. A vaccine with live germs too feeble to cause the disease | c. Contains an inactivated bacterial toxin
4. A newer vaccine that carries instructions for the body's cells | d. Made from weakened pathogens
A student claims: 'A vaccine is made by putting the whole germ into the injection.' Is the claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. Some vaccines are made from weakened or dead pathogens (such as viruses or bacteria), so they do contain the whole germ, and the claim fits those. But others are made from inactive or harmless parts of the pathogen (the tetanus shot contains an inactivated bacterial toxin), and some newer vaccines instruct our own body cells to make a harmless part of the germ; these do not contain the whole germ.
s: Verdict: partly right
Weakened or dead whole pathogens are used in some vaccines
Others use parts, an inactivated toxin or instructions to the body's cells, not the whole germ

questions.q:
In a village in the late 1700s, during a smallpox outbreak, a doctor notices that the dairy workers who had earlier caught cowpox, a milder disease from cows, stay well, while many of their neighbours fall ill with smallpox.
(a) Write a hypothesis that explains the doctor's observation. (1)
(b) Long after this, a worldwide vaccination campaign was run. A practice chart (simplified figures, for this question only) shows the number of countries reporting smallpox: 1960: 60; 1965: 44; 1970: 22; 1975: 6; 1979: 0. In this chart the campaign begins in 1965. By what percentage did the number fall from 1965 to 1975 (nearest whole number), and what does the chart, read with the chapter, show that mass vaccination achieved? (2)
(c) Why would noticing the dairy workers alone not be enough proof? (1)
(d) Using what the chapter says about the two viruses and about how vaccines work, explain why material from a milder disease could protect against a deadly one. (1)
questions.a: (a) Something in the material from cowpox blisters protects people from smallpox. (b) Fall = 44 - 6 = 38 countries; 38 / 44 x 100 = 86%. The fall begins with the 1965 campaign and reaches zero in 1979: mass vaccination eventually eradicated smallpox worldwide, so no country reported it any more. (c) The dairy workers might differ from their neighbours in other ways (for example, less contact with smallpox patients), so the observation shows a link but not that cowpox itself gives the protection; more evidence is needed, such as records showing that people given cowpox material stay free of smallpox. (d) The chapter says the two viruses are likely related. Like any vaccine, the cowpox material trained the immune system to recognise and attack the germ, and because the viruses are related, the trained immune system could also fight smallpox.
s: Part (a): cowpox blister material protects against smallpox
Part (b): 38 of 44 countries, a fall of 86%
Part (b): mass vaccination from 1965 led to smallpox being eradicated (zero countries by 1979)
Part (c): the workers may differ in other ways, so a link is not proof that cowpox gives the protection
Part (d): related viruses, so immunity trained by cowpox also fights smallpox

questions.q: A graph of the number of countries reporting smallpox shows a vaccine campaign marked in 1965, after which the number falls year by year until 1979, when smallpox is marked as eradicated. Which conclusion does the chapter support?
questions.a: Mass vaccination stopped its spread until no country had cases
o: Mass vaccination stopped its spread until no country had cases
Antibiotics given after 1965 cured smallpox patients in every country
Smallpox germs slowly weakened into cowpox after the campaign
The vaccine cured the people who were already sick in 1965

questions.q: Differentiate between how a vaccine and an antibiotic are used against disease, with the right moment for each.
questions.a: A vaccine is preventive: it is given before a person falls ill, to train the immune system so the disease does not happen. An antibiotic is a treatment: it is given after a person is already ill with a bacterial infection, to kill the bacteria.
s: Vaccine: preventive, given before illness to train the immune system
Antibiotic: treatment, given after a bacterial infection to kill bacteria

questions.q: The answer to a question is: 'Because vaccines protect people of all ages, from infants to the elderly.' Write a question set in a real situation for which this is the answer, and explain the answer in two sentences using the chapter.
questions.a: Example question: 'Seventy-year-old Dadi says vaccines are only for babies and refuses one offered at the health centre. Why is she mistaken?' Explanation: a vaccine trains the immune system to recognise and attack a harmful germ, and the chapter says vaccines protect people of all ages, from infants to the elderly, against many serious diseases. So an older person can still gain acquired immunity from a vaccine, and also protects the people around her.
s: A question where someone doubts that a vaccine is useful at their age
Vaccines train the immune system against a germ
The chapter says they protect all ages, infants to the elderly

questions.q:
Your neighbour in Patna does not want the measles vaccine for her baby. She says: 'My baby is healthy and eats well, so her natural immunity is enough.'
(a) Differentiate between the natural immunity she means and the protection a vaccine gives.
(b) Using what the chapter says about how often different people fall sick, explain why good health and diet alone cannot assure her that the baby is safe.
questions.a: (a) Immunity is the body's natural ability to fight diseases. A vaccine gives acquired immunity: it trains the immune system to recognise and attack the measles germ in advance, before the baby ever meets it. (b) The chapter notes that some people get sick more often than others even when living in a similar environment, so being healthy and well fed does not guarantee protection. Without the vaccine, the baby's immune system would meet measles for the first time only when she catches it, and she may fall ill.
s: Part (a): natural ability to fight disease versus acquired immunity trained by the vaccine in advance
Part (b): natural immunity varies between people, so a healthy diet cannot guarantee protection

questions.q:
Last winter, 30 children with measles in a district could not get a hospital bed. The district health board now has money for one of two plans before next winter's measles season: (i) vaccinating all children who have not yet had the measles vaccine, or (ii) adding 50 hospital beds to treat children who fall ill with measles.
(a) State one thing each plan can do that the other cannot. (2)
(b) Which plan also reduces the spread of measles to people who are not reached by it? Explain. (1)
(c) The bed shortage last winter is a real argument for plan (ii). Weigh it against plan (i), decide which plan the board should choose, and say what it should still do for children who fall ill anyway. (2)
questions.a: (a) Vaccination prevents children from getting measles in the first place, by training their immune systems in advance; beds cannot stop anyone from falling ill. Beds give care to children who are already sick; a vaccine cannot, because vaccines are preventive, not curative. (b) Vaccination. Vaccinated children are protected and are unlikely to catch measles and pass it on, so it reduces the spread of infection and protects the people around them too, including those not vaccinated; beds do not stop spread. (c) The vaccination plan. Extra beds would help only the children who are already ill, and the shortage came from the number of cases; vaccination spares children the disease altogether and cuts its spread, so fewer children fall ill and the existing beds are more likely to be enough. Prevention is better than cure. But some children will still fall ill (for example, before they are vaccinated), so the board should still see that they get treatment at existing hospitals and are isolated to protect others.
s: Vaccination prevents illness; beds cannot
Beds treat the sick; a vaccine cannot cure
Vaccination reduces spread and protects others
Chooses vaccination, answering the bed-shortage case: fewer cases means fewer beds needed
Still provides treatment and isolation for those who fall ill

questions.q:
After a hepatitis A outbreak in a village near Mandya, the health team checked all 200 children. 150 had received the hepatitis A vaccine last year; 50 had not. Of the vaccinated children, 3 fell ill; of the unvaccinated children, 27 fell ill. The team also found sewage leaking into the village's main well, which all 2,000 villagers use.
(a) What percentage of the unvaccinated children, and of the vaccinated children, fell ill?
(b) Besides vaccination, the chapter lists one more preventive measure for hepatitis A. Name it and explain why it would also protect people who are not vaccinated.
(c) Next year the panchayat can pay for only one plan: vaccinating the 50 children born or arriving since the drive, or repairing the well and supplying safe, boiled drinking water for the whole village. Weigh both using your answers and decide.
questions.a: (a) Unvaccinated: 27 / 50 x 100 = 54%. Vaccinated: 3 / 150 x 100 = 2%. (b) Drinking boiled water. Hepatitis A spreads through contaminated water and food, so boiled, clean water removes the pathogen before it is swallowed, whoever drinks it, vaccinated or not. (c) The vaccine has strong evidence in its favour: 2% of vaccinated children fell ill against 54% of unvaccinated, so the 50 new children would be well protected. But the well-and-water plan removes the source of the outbreak for all 2,000 villagers, adults included, and the same clean water also prevents other water-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid. So the water plan is the better single choice, with the new children vaccinated when money next allows.
s: Part (a): 54% and 2%
Part (b): boiled drinking water, which removes the pathogen for everyone
Part (c): weighs the 2% against 54% evidence against protecting the whole village from the source, and chooses the water plan

questions.q: Four patients visit a Kolkata clinic. For which of them could an antibiotic be a suitable treatment, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Sushil, who has tuberculosis
o: Sushil, who has tuberculosis
Mohan, who has malaria fever
Leela, who has dengue fever
Farah, who has influenza

questions.q:
Match each disease in Column I with the statement in Column II that explains whether an antibiotic can treat it.
Column I | Column II
1. Typhoid | a. Caused by a virus, so antibiotics do not work
2. Dengue | b. Not caused by any pathogen; managed by medication and lifestyle change
3. Malaria | c. Caused by bacteria, so antibiotics can work
4. Diabetes | d. Caused by a protozoan, so antibiotics do not work

Scientists test a new chemical that kills bacteria by destroying a structure found in bacterial cells and, equally, in human cells. Using how the chapter says antibiotics work, why would they reject it as an antibiotic?
questions.a: Antibiotics must target bacterial parts unlike human cells
o: Antibiotics must target bacterial parts unlike human cells
Antibiotics must train the immune system instead of killing
Any chemical that kills bacteria is sure to breed resistance
It could kill protozoa too, and antibiotics must spare them

questions.q:
Sumit and his cousin both catch a throat infection at a wedding. Sumit's body fights it off in two days without any medicine. His cousin's gets worse, and the doctor asks for a test to find the pathogen before deciding on an antibiotic.
(a) What protected Sumit without medicine?
(b) Why does the doctor need to know the pathogen before giving the cousin an antibiotic?
questions.a: (a) His immune system: the natural ability of his body to fight diseases (immunity). (b) Antibiotics kill bacteria and work only against bacterial infections; they do not work against viruses or protozoa. If the infection is caused by a virus, an antibiotic would not help and taking it when not required would only add to antibiotic resistance.
s: Part (a): his immune system (immunity)
Part (b): antibiotics work only on bacteria, not viruses or protozoa, so the pathogen decides

questions.q: True or False? 'Antibiotic resistance means that a person's body has got used to an antibiotic, so the medicine no longer works in that person.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. Resistance is a change in the bacteria, not in the person's body: bacteria that were earlier killed by a given antibiotic survive and multiply despite treatment with it. Such resistant bacteria can also spread to other people, and through animal food products and crops grown in soil with manure, where the same antibiotic will fail against them too.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the bacteria survive and multiply despite the antibiotic; it is the bacteria that resist

questions.q: A lab assistant finds an old dish of bacteria left near the sink. A patch of mould has grown on it, and in a ring around the mould no bacteria are growing, though they cover the rest of the dish. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.a: The mould gives out a substance that kills the bacteria
o: The mould gives out a substance that kills the bacteria
The bacteria near the mould have become resistant
The bacteria died because the dish was left near a sink
The mould is a virus that has eaten the bacteria around it

questions.q:
A doctor in Varanasi prescribes Anjali 3 antibiotic tablets a day for 5 days for a bacterial throat infection. She takes 2 tablets a day for 3 days, feels better and stops, keeping the rest in a drawer. A week later her fever returns. Her mother says: 'Nine tablets are left. That is three more days at three a day, so taking them now will finish the course the doctor wrote.'
(a) How many tablets were prescribed, and what percentage of the course did Anjali actually take?
(b) What may have happened to the bacteria that her incomplete course did not kill?
(c) Check the mother's arithmetic, then decide whether Anjali should take the leftover tablets or go back to the doctor. Weigh the mother's argument against the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 3 x 5 = 15 tablets prescribed; she took 2 x 3 = 6, which is 6 / 15 x 100 = 40%. (b) Some bacteria survived; with an incomplete dose they can develop resistance to that antibiotic and multiply, which may be why the fever returned. (c) The arithmetic is right: 15 - 6 = 9 tablets, which is 3 days at 3 a day. But finishing the old course a week late is not the same as the course she was given: the bacteria that survived may now be resistant to this antibiotic, so the tablets may not kill them, and if the new fever has another cause (for example a virus) the antibiotic would not work and would be taken when not required, adding to resistance. So she should go back to the doctor, who can find the cause and decide on treatment.
s: Part (a): 15 tablets, 6 taken, 40%
Part (b): surviving bacteria may develop resistance and multiply
Part (c): accepts the arithmetic (9 = 3 days x 3) but chooses the doctor, since the bacteria may now resist the drug or the fever may not be bacterial

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Penicillin, discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928, was the first antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections.
Reason (R): Antibiotics do not work against diseases caused by viruses.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
(a) Why can a patient swallow an antibiotic that kills the bacteria in her throat without it killing her own throat cells?
(b) Using (a), explain why the same antibiotic does nothing against the influenza virus.
questions.a: (a) Antibiotics target parts of bacterial cells that are different from human or other animal cells, so they attack the bacteria and leave her own cells alone. (b) Influenza is caused by a virus, not a bacterium, so the bacterial cell parts that the antibiotic attacks are not there to be attacked; the chapter states that antibiotics do not work against viruses.
s: Part (a): they target bacterial cell parts unlike human cells
Part (b): a virus is not a bacterium, so the antibiotic has nothing to target

questions.q: Deepak was prescribed a seven-day antibiotic course for a bacterial infection, felt better on day three and stopped. What is the chapter's main worry about this?
questions.a: Surviving bacteria may become resistant to that antibiotic
o: Surviving bacteria may become resistant to that antibiotic
His body may get used to the drug, so it stops working in him
The surviving bacteria may change into viruses no drug can kill
The tablets he took will now act as a vaccine against bacteria

questions.q: A vet in Haryana claims: 'Giving antibiotics to farm animals when they do not need them can make infections in people harder to treat.' Is the claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: Right. Unneeded antibiotics in animals lead to resistance developing in the bacteria inside those animals. Resistant bacteria then reach people through animal food products, and through manure or animal faeces in crop fields and the crops grown there. Once resistant bacteria are in people, infections are harder to treat.
s: Verdict: right
Unneeded antibiotics produce resistant bacteria in animals
They reach people through animal food or manure and crops, making infections harder to treat

questions.q:
A bacteriologist studying harmful bacteria finds, on a dish that had been thrown aside, a patch of mould. Around the mould is a clear ring with no bacteria, while bacteria cover the rest of the dish.
(a) What inference does the clear ring support, and why does the ring's position matter? (1)
(b) Using ordinary fair-test reasoning, design a test to check that a substance released by the mould, and not the mould itself touching the bacteria, kills them. Say what you would do. (2)
(c) What result of your test would support the inference? (1)
(d) Many bacteria that such substances once killed now survive them. If the dish had held such bacteria, would a clear ring still appear? Explain using the chapter's meaning of antibiotic resistance. (1)
questions.a: (a) The mould releases a substance that kills the bacteria (or stops them growing). The ring sits around the mould, where the substance would spread out from it, while bacteria grow normally away from it, so the effect comes from the mould. (b) Any fair test that keeps the mould itself away from the bacteria while its substance can reach them, with an identical comparison dish, is accepted. For example: grow the mould in a liquid, remove all the mould so only the liquid is left, and put some of it on a fresh dish of the same bacteria; put plain liquid (that never held mould) on a second, identical dish. Another sound design keeps the mould behind a barrier that only liquid can pass, beside a dish with the barrier but no mould. (c) Bacteria die or do not grow where the substance from the mould reached them, but grow normally on the comparison dish. This shows that a substance released into the liquid, not the mould itself, kills them. (This is how Fleming's 1928 chance observation led to penicillin, the first antibiotic.) (d) No clear ring, or a much smaller one: resistant bacteria are bacteria that were earlier killed by a given antibiotic but now survive and multiply despite it, so they would grow right up to the mould.
s: Part (a): the mould releases a bacteria-killing substance; the ring centred on the mould shows this
Part (b): any fair test in which only the substance from the mould, not the mould itself, reaches fresh bacteria
Part (b): an identical comparison dish without the substance
Part (c): bacteria stop growing only where the substance reached them
Part (d): no ring, as resistant bacteria survive and multiply despite the substance

questions.q: A clinic's list of patients for the day: typhoid, malaria, cholera, dengue, influenza and tuberculosis, one patient each. The number of these patients whose disease an antibiotic could treat is ___. (Write the number in digits.)

A child in a Pune hospital has a bacterial skin infection of a kind that antibiotic X cured easily ten years ago. This time X fails, then antibiotic Y fails, and only antibiotic Z clears it after three weeks in hospital.
(a) What has changed in the bacteria, according to the chapter's meaning of antibiotic resistance?
(b) Which effects of resistance named in the chapter does this case already show, and what worse effects could follow if Z also stopped working?
questions.a: (a) Bacteria of this kind, which X and Y used to kill, now survive and multiply despite treatment with those antibiotics; the change is in the bacteria. (b) Already shown: a common infection that has become harder to treat, and a prolonged illness (three weeks in hospital). If Z also failed, the chapter warns of a higher risk of complications and even death.
s: Part (a): the bacteria now survive and multiply despite X and Y
Part (b): harder to treat and prolonged illness now; complications or death if Z fails

Statement 1: Resistant bacteria can spread from a hospital into the community when patients go home.
Statement 2: Resistant bacteria that develop in animals can reach people through animal food products.
Statement 3: Resistant bacteria can reach a person only through direct contact with an infected patient.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 1 only
All three statements

questions.q:
The Sharma family has never visited a hospital and keeps no animals, yet two family members now carry antibiotic-resistant bacteria.
(i) Trace one route, in two steps, by which resistant bacteria from a patient in a city hospital could have reached them through people.
(ii) Trace one route by which resistant bacteria could have reached them without passing through any person.
questions.a: (i) Step 1: in the hospital, resistant bacteria spread from the patient to other patients, directly, through dirty surfaces or through healthcare workers. Step 2: patients carrying them go home and spread the resistant bacteria into the community, from where they reach the Sharmas. (ii) Resistant bacteria develop in farm animals given antibiotics; they reach the soil of a crop field through manure or animal faeces, and the family eats the crop produce, so the bacteria reach their digestive system. (Animal food products such as milk or eggs from such animals are another route.)
s: Route (i) step 1: spread inside the hospital via patients, surfaces or healthcare workers
Route (i) step 2: patients go home and spread them in the community
Route (ii): animals to manure to soil to crops (or animal food products) to the family

questions.q: A district's health board lists actions to slow antibiotic resistance. Which action does NOT belong on the list?
questions.a: Routinely giving antibiotics to healthy farm animals
o: Routinely giving antibiotics to healthy farm animals
Asking patients to finish the full prescribed course
Cleaning hospital surfaces and hands between patients
Not using antibiotics for viral colds and influenza

questions.q:
A hospital in Kozhikode keeps this log for one ward.
Day 1: Patient in bed 4 is found to carry bacteria that survive both antibiotics the hospital stocks.
Day 3: A nurse dresses the bed 4 patient's wound, then the bed 5 patient's wound, without washing her hands.
Day 6: The bed 5 patient carries the same bacteria.
Day 8: The bed 4 patient goes home. Day 15: his daughter carries the same bacteria.
Three other patients in the ward have a different bacterial infection that the hospital's two antibiotics no longer clear but a new, third antibiotic does. The hospital now plans to buy this third antibiotic and give it to every patient in the ward 'to be safe'.
(a) What name does the chapter give to bacteria behaving like those in bed 4?
(b) By what route did the bacteria reach bed 5?
(c) By what route did they reach the daughter?
(d) Say what is sound in the plan, find two flaws in it, and redesign it using the log.
questions.a: (a) Antibiotic-resistant bacteria (antibiotic resistance). (b) Indirectly through a healthcare worker, the nurse, who moved from bed 4 to bed 5 without washing her hands. (c) The patient went home and spread the resistant bacteria to the community, here his daughter. (d) Sound: the three patients with the other infection do need the new antibiotic, since the old two no longer clear it. Flaw 1: giving an antibiotic to patients who do not need it is the kind of unneeded use that lets bacteria develop resistance, so the new drug could soon fail too. Flaw 2: the plan does nothing about the route the log shows, the nurse's unwashed hands and the patient going home carrying the bacteria. Redesign: give the new antibiotic only to patients who are ill with a bacterial infection it treats (the three patients, and bed 4 or 5 only if ill and the drug works on their bacteria), and enforce handwashing and surface cleaning between patients, so the spread is blocked.
s: Part (a): antibiotic-resistant bacteria
Part (b): through the healthcare worker's unwashed hands
Part (c): the patient went home and spread it in the community
Part (d): the plan rightly treats the three ill patients, but unneeded use breeds resistance and it ignores the spread route; give it only to those who need it and enforce handwashing and cleaning

questions.q: Kiran's grandfather has a serious bacterial infection. He wants to treat it only with herbal oils from a traditional system and refuses the antibiotic his doctor prescribed. Give two points from the chapter that he should weigh.
questions.a: (1) Traditional systems such as Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani use natural substances like herbs, oils and minerals, and can help with some conditions and everyday well-being, but they may not be effective for all diseases and at all stages. (2) Antibiotics kill the bacteria causing infections and have saved millions of lives, so for a serious bacterial infection the prescribed antibiotic, taken correctly, matters.
s: Traditional systems may not work for all diseases and at all stages
Antibiotics kill disease-causing bacteria and have saved millions of lives

questions.q: Lalit has dengue. His friend says that a very strong antibiotic, taken in a large dose, will surely cure him. Show why no dose of antibiotic can cure his dengue, and say what harm taking it could do.
questions.a: Dengue is caused by a virus. Antibiotics work only against bacterial infections because they target parts of bacterial cells that are different from human or other animal cells, so they do not work against viruses, whatever the dose. Taking an antibiotic when it is not required is indiscriminate use, which helps antibiotic resistance develop in bacteria.
s: Dengue is caused by a virus
Antibiotics target bacterial cell parts, so they do not work on viruses at any dose
Unneeded use encourages antibiotic resistance

questions.q: Design a five-point poster for your school's health week titled 'Keep Antibiotics Working'. Each point should be a short instruction for families, followed by the reason from the chapter. Cover: taking antibiotics when they are not needed, stopping a course early, illnesses they cannot treat, farm animals, and hospitals.
questions.a: Any five sound points, e.g. (1) Do not take antibiotics when they are not required: unneeded use lets resistance develop in the bacteria in your body. (2) Do not stop at the first sign of feeling better; take the full dose: an incomplete dose leaves bacteria that can survive and become resistant. (3) Do not expect antibiotics to treat colds, flu or dengue: they work only against bacteria, not viruses or protozoa. (4) Do not give antibiotics to healthy farm animals: resistant bacteria develop in the animals and reach us through animal food products and through manure in crop fields. (5) In hospitals, keep hands and surfaces clean: resistant bacteria spread through dirty surfaces and healthcare workers to other patients, and then home to the community. Overall, resistance makes infections harder to treat and can lead to complications, prolonged illness or death.
s: Not when unneeded, with reason
Full dose, not stopping early, with reason
Not for viral or protozoan illness, with reason
Farm animals, with the food and crop route
Hospitals: clean hands and surfaces, with the spread route
